segments.text: bureaucrats in India have managed to turn the rather unglamorous business of regulation into a national conversation quite like Tukaram Munde.

As Maharashtra's Food and Drug Administration Commissioner, he has forced food safety out of government files and into public consciousness, taking on famous restaurants, powerful businesses, and even, lately, some of India's biggest film stars, fearlessly.
And that's made him a public hero.
His enforcement drive has made millions of consumers ask a simple question.
What exactly are we eating, buying, trusting, consuming?
And now Tukaram Munde is training his gaze on something even more fundamental to our health.
What happens when we are admitted to hospitals, when we go to doctors, when we go to clinics?
His FDA survey has uncovered extraordinary markups on everyday medical consumables.
An IV set procured, for example, for about 11 rupees carrying an MRP of 325.
A syringe bought for 6 rupees, 75 paise.
You pay about 57 rupees.
In some cases, the gap between procurement price and MRP exceeds 2,800% according to the findings of this man.
Munday has now asked the national pricing regulator to get in and fix this.
And none other than Tukaram Munde himself joins me now.
Mr. Munde, good to have you here on NDTV.
Thank you very much for your time, sir.
Thank you.
Thank you so much.
My first question straight off on the issue at hand, sir.
Let me begin with the medical devices investigation that you have initiated.
You've uncovered markups which most people in the back of their minds thought it must be true.
Yes, we are paying extra for medical devices but people are frankly shocked by what you have uncovered.
Markups running into hundreds and even thousands of percent.

Is this in your understanding sir, simply excessive profit or do you believe you have uncovered a systematic rocket, racket because here you are talking about IV, syringes, basic medical equipment sir
So, we have to understand it in a context of hospitalization.
These are basically medical consumables which are administered and used when the patient is admitted in hospital or hospitalized in IPDA.
So, these consumables are used for treatment purposes, that is not something which is non-essential.
It is essential without that treatment cannot take place, whether it is syringes or whether it is IV or whether it is nebulizers, these things are used.
There was actually a complaint to me and said people had approached me, the hospitals are charging more.
If it is charging more than AMRP, we can take actions, we are authorized to do that.
But if it is as per the AMRP, we are not authorized to take any action because it is as per the legal norms.
So, what we did was basically to look at the data available with the various hospitals.
It will be difficult to call a survey but actually it's actually a data which have procured from the hospitals themselves.
So, we look at the consumables and we found that we took multiple hospitals in MMR regions and beyond MMR region also.
So, it's not a data of just one hospital, it's multiple hospitals.
And what we found is that the MRP which is printed, which is available in the hospital, and the hospital procurement price, there is a huge gap.
And that gap is not explainable at least to our minds, we discuss and deliberate internally also.
And that's what we found that this gap of running from 150% to up to 2800% needs to be explained properly.
Now if that product can be purchased by hospital at say 11 rupees and the price MRP is at 325, they need an explanation for that.

and that is where this markup issue has come up that is where trade regulation trade pricing regulation needs to come up that is where transparency needs to come in and that is why on these findings we have
reported to the NPPA, which looks into this issue.
To look into the issue transparently, maybe it needs to concern all the stakeholders.
And along with that, whether it needs to be brought under DCPO, Drug Control Price Order, which is under the Act of Essential Commodities Act 1955.
This current DCPO is of 2013.
Whether this needs to be brought under it or not, that is one consideration, one recommendation.
Second is, whether the trade, the pricing regulation should be considered or not, that is second.
Third one is, the industry needs to be consulted.
what can be done about it and of course transparency.

So all the stakeholders whether it's a consumer, whether it's a hospital or whether it's a manufacturer along with the regulators needs to be taken into consideration and the interest of all transparently need to be protected.
So yes there is a gap whether it can be termed as a systemic exploitation or not
MPPA will come out once the consultations are there and the views of all the stakeholders are taken into consideration.
I want to explore a little bit more in detail sir about this specific example you have taken.
Take for example the intravenous or the IV sets which are one of the most commonly used medical consumables.

11 rupees to procure, 325 rupees MRP, by your understanding, you are asking for transparency but by your understanding sir, who is actually pocketing the difference, the manufacturer, the distributor, the hospital or you know everyone is just sharing this enormous markup, can you tell us what your investigation is showing?
That is, yeah, that investigation who is sharing what is very difficult to determine at my level as of now.
But it is not passing on to consumer that is for sure because consumer was priced at 325 as per the MRP.
Whereas the hospital has got at very very lower price.
Now that definitely is between the hospitals, manufacturers, distributor, whatever their arrangement might be, we have not looked into it because we are not

looking at that aspect as of now but further details once there is a stakeholder consultation and NPPA goes into details further details it can come up with that but it is for sure if hospital gets at that price it means
325 MRP is not reasonable.
That's what it is very very clear.
And the transparency needs to be there, consumer needs to know, regulator also needs to know how it has been marked up at that level.
If that same product is sold to hospital at such a low level, why it is marked up at 325?
The percentage difference of 2800% is beyond comprehension on face of it.
So, where that profit is going needs to be looked into.
How it has been marked up at that level also needs to be looked into.
That's why our recommendation, whether to bring it under DCPO or whether there has to be trade regulation about pricing has to be there.
These are the issues to be considered by NPPA.
That's what we have recommended.
Yeah.
So, you've written to the National Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority, sir.

But by your understanding what happens now, you know, can you give the patients who are watching from across the country a concrete sense of what action you want from the center and how quickly in your view do you think prices could actually change if they will at all.
See, there is a system in place in the sense that essential medicines are regulated by prices.
So, there is NPP has guidelines about it.
The DCPO order is there.
And every year a particular percentage of increases allowed.
That is the standard procedure.
But non-essential medicines are not regulated by this.
And that is where the issue comes in.
So, whether this should be considered under essential commodities or not, according to us, I think because it is essential, it is not alternative
available there when you are admitted these things are consumed on daily basis by the hospitals for treatment purposes.
So in our considered view you have given the recommendation to NPPA.
Now whether trade regulation or it should be brought under DCPO or there is some other mechanism monitoring as surveillance has to be more stringent.
All these are the considerations point for NPPA that's what we are deliberating upon.
Now, how much time it will require?
Difficult for me to say.
NPPA will definitely look into it.
I have also had interaction with the concerned department and they are very positive about it.
I think deliberations have already started.
But at the end of the day, because what we do is we are implementing two acts here.
One is Drug and Cosmetic Act, 1940.
and rules there under and there is essential commodity act 1955 under which DCPO is issued by the government of India by NPPA.
Now the call has to be taken whether to brought it under the umbrella of DCPO or not or whether you have to go for trade regulation about the pricing and what is to be done.
But I think government and department definitely seized up the matter.
This having the complaints from consumer organizations also over a period of time and that's why we looked into it.
What we did was basically look into it very very impartially, very very transparently so that we have the data.
and we took a sample of many hospitals within MMR and beyond MMR also.
So, as a result, it's not something which is happening in a particular hospital.
It is across hospitals it is happening and this really needs to be looked into and we need to look it very very hard.
Because hospitals and the manufacturers, I am sure you have seen Mr. Munde, they are pushing back.
They will argue that, you know, procurement cost is not the final cost of delivering healthcare.
Where does Tukaram Munde draw the line between legitimate business and exploitation?
Because they will push back and say, you are taking something that is essentially legal and calling it exploitation.
Where would you draw that line, sir?
I don't have the authority to decide the price.
I can come in picture if they are selling at more than MRP.
That's why I could not take action or I will not take action because legally they are within their rights to sell a product within MRP.
So that's why we have not taken any action against either the hospital or for that matter the manufacturer and seller.

So where the ball is now in NPPA they have to decide whether it to be bought under the umbrella of essential commodity as or DCPO or trade regulation about pricing has to be there because when the particular MRP is arrived at there is a procedure for that how much actually is the expenditure how much profit margin has to be there and how this MRP is fixed that's where deliberations will take place that's where the consultation and stakeholder involvement will also take place
A manufacturer may sell a particular product at lower than the MRP, but how can there be a gap of 2000 plus percentage on a particular product which is almost daily basic consumer?
Does it mean that MRP was wrongly placed or does it mean that there is something else?
That really is the crux of the matter and that's where we need to deliberate, work upon and come up with a transparent policy measures.

You know before I go on to the other issues that you are looking at closely, permit me to ask you a personal question Mr. Munday because you know the pharmaceutical healthcare industry is an entrenched industry, powerful, rich stakeholders.
I feel worried for your safety sir as a civilian, as a citizen.
You are taking on the big guys of a very entrenched industry by questioning margins which is a
in some, some would say a dangerous thing to do.
Are you worried about your safety?
You are a brave person but I feel worried about your safety, sir.
I am actually worried about the public health.
That's what my role is.
Have you, have you ever received any intimidation, any threat calls, anything of that kind?
I, because I am just wondering when you take on the big guys in this manner.
During this period?
During this, during this period as a FDA commissioner?
Yes.
No, not during this period of MTA Commissioner, no.
Okay, let's move on.
I am glad you haven't because I think people are...
you know may be nervous when they see how committed you are to what you are pursuing which I think is a good thing.
But I sincerely pray for your safety on this front.
Let me come to another part of this whole thing Mr. Munday.
Your crack down on restaurants which made the headlines a few weeks ago, you are continuing with that, that has been equally aggressive.
Cafe Mondagar is the latest, you know the famous establishment to face action under you.
Do you believe sir that there is
a much bigger food safety problem in Mumbai, Maharashtra than consumers currently realize.
You have put the spotlight on something that most people were in denial about.
Do you think the issue is far bigger than most people are willing to accept?
I think we have to look at it not as a food safety issue, but a public health issue.
And that's the context we have to look into.
Unless we look into this issue as a public health issue at large, rather than just looking at adulteration or substandard or food safety issue, that will not lead to anywhere.
The objective of Food Safety and Standards Authority of India Act 2006 is ultimately to improve
the public health by providing science-based standards and regulations about food.
That's the whole issue.
Now coming to whether it's unsafe or substandard, let me put in a context.
Last three months, for around 100 days, we have inspected around 12,000 established in the food sector.
Whether it's milk, milk products, and hotels, restaurants, eateries, all put together.
Out of these 12,000 inspections, more than 5,200 establishments have been issued improvement notices.
It means there were non-compliances.
where improvement was needed.
And around 600 odd, 603 out of these, where licenses were suspended forthwith.
Now why these licenses were suspended forthwith is basically because of non-compliances, particularly in schedule 4 of the regulations.
That is Licensing and Registration Regulation 2011, that is schedule 4, which is non-negotiable.
That's where the forthwith suspensions come in.
Now these are the non-compliances, it means there is an issue.
Now out of 12,000, if you are looking at improvement notices plus this one, it comes around 5,800.
Almost 50% food businesses, we found these deficiencies or non-compliances.
So, the answer to your question is, yes, there is an issue.
Now, how much?
Yes, it will vary from place to place, restaurant to restaurant, business to business.
There is no uniform pattern as such.
But why has this been happening?
I think we have to again contextualize this.
Because before this act came into existence, we were having the act of prevention of food adulteration act.
The focus of preventing the adulteration.
So the focus was not on preparing standard and safe food.
That's where we have actually changed the context from preventing adulteration to worse going a culture where it speaks of safe and standard food.
So standards are let down.
Now when these new standards were let down and these standards are coming over a period of time, regulations are coming over a period of time after 2011, this is where culture
of food business operator needed to change, they have been changing, they have been making changes.
Same way the culture of work culture of regulator needs to undergo change.
That has been going on over a period of time.
So the testing lab has also been, has also go down the line in the same manner.
So as individuals, as consumers also we need to look at it from safety and standard point of view, not just adulteration point of view or
from the taste point of view.
So, we need these food habits which we have over a period of 100 years of change.
Look at the context, in larger context says independence till now.
See, at the time of independence, our disease burden of communicable diseases was in the range of 65% to 70%.
and remaining are non-communicable.
Today, we have non-communicable or NCDs, what we call, in the range of 65% and communicable has gone around 30% of the total.
The ratio has reversed.
And one of the major reasons why NCDs have gone up is what we consume.
That's why we have been able to see obesity issues have risen up, the cardiovascular disease have gone up, cancer and BP and other lifestyle diseases have gone up.
This has direct linkages to what we consume.

And I think we need to be much much aware, we need to be much much stringent about our food habits, particularly about high in fat, salt and sugar products which we consume over a period of time has increased.
And I think with packaged industry, packaged foods,
what we are doing is looking at the brand or looking at just best before expiry or cost and not looking at the ingredients, that is causing lot of issues.

So yes, there is the issue of food safety, there is issue of food standards, but to brand it that everything is wrong is also incorrect because in more than 50% of the cases we found have been complying with.
So, it's an issue.
We need to address it and we need to address it from public health point of view which is not just a point of view of food safety and the standard food.
I take your point sir.
Let's come to some other you know missions of yours.
You've gone after some big stars, brand ambassadors, people like Shah Rukh Khan, Ajay Devgan, Tiger Shroff over the
you know the Vimal Elaichi campaign, you know these are big celebrities.
What is your view on that?
You know the moral and legal responsibility of endorsers and brand ambassadors.
Where does it begin when the product being advertised is technically not the prohibited product?
There are clearly advertising regulations as per the Food and Safety Act.
There are 2018 regulations which talk about advertising.
It talks about who is the advertiser and there is a responsibility very specifically casted upon the person or institution who is advertising.
So to say that it is only a producer or a manufacturer is wrong because there is very very clear let down rules and regulations.
Section 24 of that speaks up it and the advertising and regulations also speak about it.
So there is a responsibility casted upon the person or the person who is advertising it including to take a due diligence about what he or she is endorsing.
They have to go for due diligence.
It has to be as per the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India regulations, rules.
It is very very clearly stated.
So, to say that it is not upon them is wrong, legally incorrect.
Not only morally but legally I am talking about because I am here a person as a regulator.
So, they have highlighted and that is why we have issued the notices.
According to you they may be stars but according to me they are only advertisers in this case.
So I am looking at them as here violators of the law and the law will take its own course.
That's why we have started taking action.
So that's where we found that they were involved in surrogate advertisement, the food product or food item which is prohibited in the state of Maharashtra.
has been advertised by them and that's where the law is breached.
That's why we are taking this action as per the law.
Mr. Munde, have the teams of Shahrukh Khan or Ajay Devgan or Tiger Shroff or any of the others who you have issued notice to, have they responded to you?
Have they tried to communicate with you, establish contact with you about this?
Is there a conversation directly with them or their teams?
Out of these three notices, we have got response from two.
One is yet to come.
And we are proceeding further on that.
Because these two responses which are there, exactly they stand what you stated earlier, that is the responsibility of the manufacturer, not us.
That is what they have taken.
So, we are giving them hearing, my officer assistant commissioner who issued the notices will be giving the hearing.
In one case where they have not responded, we are starting the adjudicating and prosecution proceeding as per the act.
Who has responded and who has not responded if you can share with us sir?
I exactly don't remember of the three, only two have responded, one have not responded that much I remember.
I remember because that is with the assistant commissioner.
So, that's the information with me.
Has Shah Rukh Khan's team responded?
I am exactly not exactly known which two have responded, which one have not responded.
Most likely he have not responded but I am not too sure about it.
Okay, okay.
You are saying that you are not sure if he has responded.
I will leave that aside.
Sir, there is another side to the Tukaram Munde story.
You've seen the Bombay High Court's recent words about you.

They've used extraordinarily strong language about the FDA's action asking whether you thought you were a lord who could do anything and criticizing what it saw as undue haste and failures of natural justice.
How did you see that language being used for you by the Bombay High Court, sir?
See, whatever High Court says, we take it very seriously.
We look into our processes.
We look into whether my officer or somebody has made error in judgment or made any mistake, whether in the process or in application or interpretation of the provisions of the law.
And most of the cases, we have found that we have not violated the law.
We are actually following the due process.
Now, some of these statements were made in the court during interactions or the proceedings.
They have not come on the record.
Only one case where the fine was imposed on my officer in Pune case is on the record.
Otherwise, High Court has actually gone on the record to appreciate our efforts.
The way we have been implementing, it is on the record.
Now, wherever these occasions occur,
We look into it.
If my officer or somebody has committed some error, we definitely rectify it.
We are open to it.
Because we are as a public servant, definitely must be above any criticism without making any mistakes.
So, that's our stand.
However, we have again and again said that we are following the due process.
We will follow the due process and we will go wherever we think that
Our point of view or facts were not taken into consideration while dealing with the case.
We point it out, we bring it to the notice of the court.
In the case where we are fine, we are preferring an appeal before Supreme Court.

Because we think that we are wrong, we are right and because that was a food poisoning case, the sample of that food has also been found unsafe and that was not according to us taken into consideration.
So, that is why we are preferring an appeal before the Supreme Court.
But by and large, there are some incidences where these issues were raised and we have looked into it.
But very, very clearly, if there is an issue, we take it seriously.
If we think that we have done the right thing, we proceed accordingly.
That's our stand.
We are committed to implement the law as it should be, in a transparent and process-oriented manner.
Mr. Munde, food safety from a public health perspective, you know, medical consumables from a consumer perspective, possibility of exploitation and lack of transparency.
Give us a sense of what your next mission is going to look like.
These two have obviously caught the country's imagination because they matter to the everyday human being.
What are you going, what is Tukaram Munde going after next?

I think it's basically as I said the overarching goal is to improve public health and to do that these are very crucial elements whether it's a food or drug or cosmetics for that matter there are multiple issues in that also we are working on that also

So ultimately, if you look at it holistically or 360 degree point of view, on the one hand, we have been saying that we need to increase our GDP on public health so that public health is taken care of.

And on the other hand, because of the public, there is WHO report and there are report by the Minister of Health and Family Welfare where it says that there is a huge loss to the GDP because of the diseases born out of food, foodborne diseases.
In 2026 there is a report by WHO which says that the deaths which occurred because of foodborne diseases, 73% of these were because of chemical contamination or chemical impact from the food.
It means that chemical contamination has taken place in the food and that is to the 73% of the foodborne disease mortality issues.
So we need to tackle it very very seriously so that our GDP also is not affected because of food business, foodborne diseases.
As unsafe food is consumed, there are issues of even mortality, morbidity, all these issues come up.
So that our GDP is not lost on the one hand and if we consume safe food and standard food and standard medicines, ultimately
the productivity will go up and expenditure on health will go down.
That is on the one hand.
On the second hand if you look at it, the more demand for pure and safe food is there, the agriculture will also get better prices.
For example, in Maharashtra in last three months time, what I have observed, milk prices have gone up for the farmers in the range of 10 to 20 rupees per litre for cow and buffalo milk.
So, that's quite a giant leap for producers of milk and milk industry.
So, it's a win-win situation if you really implement this law and to do that what I think the most important factor is the awareness among the people.
It has to be from a public movement that they need safe and standard food.
They need to question what they

eat and what they purchase so that it benefits as a consumer, it benefits as a agriculturist and it benefits as a country so that the GDP goes up, productivity goes up, diseases go down and economy grows.
That's the whole context in which we are working and it has to become a public movement so that we as a nation are a healthy nation and a better nation.

Final question Mr. Munde, you know you've acquired an image of an officer who arrives somewhere and suddenly everybody starts checking whether their licenses, kitchens and paperwork are in order and that's actually a good thing.
I am wondering why did it take a Tukaram Munde to come to awaken this in the public imagination?
What was it that Tukaram Munde has brought to the table that
All of the people before in this area have not done.
You enjoy a reputation now where people are saying Thank God there is someone like Tukaram Munde actually looking into all these things.
Why did it take someone like you sir?
What happened to all the people who came before you?
I think everybody has worked, everybody has contributed.
Maybe the scale might be different, method might be different, maybe they did not get as much visibility as my work has been getting.
So there may be multiple factors.
But I believe that everybody has put a system in place because this Act came in 2011.
Systems needed to be put in place.
My predecessors have done it.
I did not start working in the Hoyt.
There were systems, there were officers, there were procedures.
So it's not a work of me alone.
It's over a period of time this work has happened.
And it is not again me.
My all officers, whether it's a food safety officer, drug inspector, assistant commissioner, joint commissioner,
They are contributing to it.
It's not just work of Tukaramonde.
I believe that we have to understand it's a systemic effort and I believe institutions are much more important than an individual.
But given a context, what we need is more awareness among the people.
There are three major stakeholders in this area.
One is food business operators or licensees in drug sector who need to abide by and compliant with regulations and rules.
That is first.
Second is the regulator.
We need to be much more stringent because that affects the public health.
Just not an issue of unsafe or substandard food.
It is a public health issue.
And last but not least, public needs to be much more vigilant.
They need to be much more
what we call questioning what they are purchasing.
Because if you are purchasing something packaged, we have to look at the ingredients of it.
Because many a time misbranded is there, misleading advertisement or nomenclature is there.
Even on the one hand you will say that it is sugar free but when you look in the ingredients you will find the sugar content in it.
All these things are there.
So, we need to be much more aware of what exactly we are consuming because we are just not consuming.
We are actually compromising our health both physical
intellectual and growing.
That's where we need to look into.
If we are looking into this, I think we need not look at anybody, but look up to ourselves.
By looking up to ourselves in holistic manner, we will be doing lot good to ourselves, our families, community and the society at large.
You know, you've been very modest as I end this interview Mr. Munday.
You've said that the system is bigger than the individual.
I would just argue that sometimes it takes the individual to get the system to work and you've already given NDP a big headline after food and medical supplies.
Now, cosmetics could be the next thing that you work on from a public health perspective.
Is that right?
Cosmetics is in your sights now.
Cosmetic is there and I think basically health, because I think one of the major issues here is about child nutrition also.
So, we started in Maharashtra, this balanced diet in the school, I have issued complaint order, HFHS food is not available in the campus of the school or within 50 meter radius of the school.
Extending that, I am going on infant food.
Impact substitutes and milk substitutes and bottles.
That is one major area we are looking after.
So, there are multiple areas to go after.
But immediate, yes, along with medicines, drugs and this food item, infant food is the next online.
The next food is orderly issue.
And festive season, we have started taking action and I think that will make lot of impact.
on our health as well.
We wish you the very best.
Thank you very much and be safe in your activities.
We will be tracking it and thank you for your service once again and thank you for being here on NDTV.
Thank you sir.
Thank you.
Thank you.
